problem: The paragraph says 'Two dynamic ratings decide protection' and then lists three items: di/dt, dv/dt and gate charge Qg. Qg is not a protection limit; it is a drive requirement.
fix: Say 'Two dynamic ratings decide protection: di/dt and dv/dt.' Then start a new sentence: 'Gate charge Qg sets what the driver must supply on every pulse.'

problem: ITSM is described as 'the single 50 Hz half-cycle current'. The datasheet value is a peak current; without the word peak a student may use an RMS or average value.
fix: 'ITSM is the peak surge current the device can survive for one 50 Hz half-cycle in a fault.'

problem: The text presents di/dt as a rating on 'anode or drain current'. A MOSFET has no datasheet di/dt rating for drain current; the drain-current rise is set by the gate drive and circuit. The di/dt rating is mainly a thyristor/SCR rating (MOSFETs have body-diode di/dt and dv/dt limits).
fix: 'For an SCR, di/dt is the highest rate at which anode current may rise at turn-on...' and treat MOSFET drain di/dt as a circuit design limit, not a device rating.

problem: 'The resistor must be rated for this continuous pulse power, not its average DC value alone' is confusing and contradicts itself. The continuous rating of a resistor is its average power rating; the pulse/overload rating is a separate short-time check.
fix: 'The resistor's continuous power rating must exceed this average value (16 W here). Check its short-pulse overload rating separately.'

problem: 'The R-C turn-off snubber is useless without Rs' overstates the point and conflicts with Section 2 and Q4. Cs alone still limits dv/dt at turn-off; the danger is the huge turn-on discharge current through the switch.
fix: 'An R-C snubber is unsafe without Rs: Cs alone still slows the voltage rise at turn-off, but at turn-on it discharges into the switch through only stray resistance.'

where: Section 3, peak gate current formula and Quiz Q6
problem: The formula and Q6 use VGE (gate-emitter voltage) for a MOSFET. MOSFET datasheets use VGS (gate-source voltage); VGE is the IGBT term.
fix: Use VGS in the formula and in Q6 for the MOSFET example, and keep VGE for the IGBT discussion.
